transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, honestly, it's... it's been a whole situation at my job. I work as a buyer, you know, wholesale and retail, so I'm constantly dealing with a lot of moving parts—inventory, vendors, seasonal launches, all that kind of stuff. And what really made me come in today is that... well, I just can't shake this feeling. Honestly, it's more than a feeling, it's like I know it's happening. 

I know that people at work, and even some of the outside vendors I coordinate with, are actively tracking my buys. Like, they are monitoring exactly what I select, and then they're going into the system and messing with the launch numbers behind my back. It's this whole coordinated thing just to sabotage my metrics and make me look completely stupid in front of everybody. I mean, I'm putting in these purchase orders, doing everything right, and then the numbers come back completely skewed. 

I even took it to my supervisor. I sat him down and explained exactly how they're altering the data, and he pulled up all these spreadsheets and historical reports, pointing at the screens, trying to tell me that the numbers match up and that the reports don't prove anyone is tampering with anything. He spent, I don't know, like an hour trying to convince me. But it doesn't matter what those reports say because I know what they're doing. I can't shake it, and it's making it impossible to just do my job when I know they're all scheming to ruin my numbers. It's just exhausting having to watch my back every single time I place an order.
How long have you been experiencing this feeling that coworkers and vendors are tracking and tampering with your work—days, weeks, or months?

Well, it definitely hasn't been just days or weeks, I can tell you that much for sure. If I really sit down and trace it back to the very first time I noticed the numbers shifting on my reports... it’s been roughly ten months now. Yeah, about ten months. I remember exactly because it was right around the time we were prepping for the big Q3 inventory push, which is always a massive headache anyway, but that's when I first realized they were actually in the system messing with my stuff. 

Ten months of having to double and triple-check every single purchase order. And, you know, it's not just the tampering and the suspicious stuff with the coworkers either. Right around that same time, about ten months ago, that's also when the voice started. Just this... this voice that chimes in while I'm working. Like, I'll be sitting at my desk, looking at a vendor catalog or trying to finalize a wholesale buy, and the voice will just be there, warning me about what they're doing behind my back or commenting on how they're changing the metrics. 

So between the voice telling me what's going on and me actually seeing the skewed numbers with my own eyes, it’s been a solid ten months of just absolute exhaustion. And like I was saying about my supervisor, he just brushes it off like it's normal seasonal stress, pulling up those historical reports like they mean anything. But how are you supposed to just relax and do your job when you've had this going on for almost a year? It's impossible to focus when you know for a fact, for ten whole months, that you're being set up to fail and you have a voice constantly reminding you of it while you're just trying to type up an invoice.

During these past ten months, have you also gone through any stretches where you felt persistently depressed, hopeless, or lost interest in things—or on the flip side, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing little sleep?

Well, depressed... no, not really. I mean, it's stressful, like I said, but I wouldn't call it depressed. But the other thing you mentioned, about feeling elevated or energetic... yeah, actually. That definitely happens. It's not the whole ten months, but I get these stretches, you know? These periods where suddenly everything just clicks. 

It's hard to explain, but it's like... it's like the whole city is opening up for me. I'll wake up, and I don't even need that much sleep, honestly, maybe a few hours, and I'm just buzzing. My brain is firing on all cylinders, I'm thinking about new vendors, new product lines, ways to completely overhaul our inventory system because I can see all the connections that nobody else is seeing. I'll be practically vibrating with energy, ready to just conquer the entire retail market. 

But... the flip side of that, and this is where it gets tricky at work, is that I get so keyed up during those stretches. Because I see things so clearly, right? And then, if someone—like my supervisor or one of the logistics guys—if they question a purchase order I've written up, or if they tell me to slow down because I'm moving too fast for them to keep up... man, I just snap. I snap way harder than I mean to. 

Like, last month, during one of these energetic phases, I had this whole vision for the seasonal launch, and I was working on it at like 3 AM because I just couldn't turn my brain off, and the next day at the office, the inventory manager asked me why I ordered triple the usual amount of this one specific item. And instead of just explaining my rationale, I completely went off on him. I was yelling, telling him he was too slow, that he was holding me back, that he didn't understand the market trends. I was just so irritated that he couldn't see the big picture like I could. It's like my patience just completely evaporates when I'm in that zone. So yeah, I definitely get those elevated stretches, but they come with a really short fuse if anyone tries to get in my way.

During the times when you're not feeling that elevated, high-energy way—when your mood is more usual—do you still notice the voice commenting on things or still feel convinced that coworkers are tampering with your orders?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, definitely. That's the most frustrating part of the whole thing, honestly. You'd think, right? You'd think if I'm not buzzing and snapping at people, if I'm just relaxed, the rest of it would just kind of... fade out. But it doesn't. It really doesn't. 

Like, just a little while ago, I had this stretch where I finally came down from one of those massive energy kicks. I was actually sleeping normally again, getting like a solid seven or eight hours a night, not waking up at 3 AM trying to redesign the whole supply chain. I felt totally regular. I wasn't walking into the office feeling like I was running the whole market or anything like that. I was just... me. Just a regular guy doing his job, taking it one day at a time, not getting irritated with the logistics guys or anything. 

But even during that calmer stretch, which lasted for a good few weeks... it didn't stop. I spent those entire few weeks still completely believing—well, knowing, really—that people were tracking my buys. I'd sit at my desk, totally calm, well-rested, sipping my coffee, and I'd still know for a fact that they were in the system messing with my numbers. 

And the voice... man, the voice was still there, too. I remember specifically being back in the main stockroom during those few weeks. It's this big, kind of drafty room in the back where we keep all the overflow and the bulky seasonal displays, and I was just doing a routine physical count. I was feeling totally fine, totally level, just counting boxes. And right there in the stockroom, plain as day, I was still hearing the voice. It was just chiming in, commenting on what I was doing, warning me about how my coworkers were manipulating my purchase orders while I was stuck in the back room. 

So it's like, even when my mood is completely baseline and I'm not keyed up at all, I still have to deal with it. It just never really gives me a break, you know? Like, I can be having a perfectly average Tuesday, sleeping great, not feeling stressed or elevated at all, and I still have to look over my shoulder in the stockroom because I know they're tracking me and the voice is right there telling me about it. It makes you wonder what the point of even having a good night's sleep is if you're just going to walk into work and deal with the exact same sabotage, you know?
Over these full ten months, roughly how much of the time would you say you were in one of those elevated, high-energy phases versus feeling at your usual baseline mood?

Well, if I sit down and really map out the calendar in my head, you know, going back to that Q3 inventory push I was talking about earlier... it’s actually kind of wild when I add it all up. Because you'd think the calm periods would be the norm, right? Like, being at a regular baseline is how a person is supposed to spend most of their year. But looking back at it now, honestly, most of the time since this all started has been taken up by those wired stretches. 

I mean, the vast majority of the ten months, really. It's just been these long, drawn-out blocks of time where I'm just going a hundred miles an hour, overworking myself, staying up all night pouring over wholesale catalogs, feeling completely overconfident like I can predict the whole market, and just being so irritable and hard to slow down. Like, I'll have a stretch that lasts for months on end where I'm just locked into that zone, snapping at the warehouse managers if they can't keep up with my pace. 

And then the calmer periods, the times when I'm just at my baseline like I was talking about when I was doing the physical counts in the stockroom... those are actually pretty short in comparison. They're really just little blips in between. Maybe a couple of weeks here or there where I can finally sleep a full night and I'm not biting someone's head off over a late shipment. But then, bam, I'm right back into the high-energy stuff. 

So if you're asking for a breakdown, it's heavily, heavily skewed. It's like my brain just decided that being constantly revved up and ready to overhaul the entire retail system is my new default setting, and being regular is just a quick vacation. I mean, spending most of the last ten months just totally wired... it really takes a toll on you. You'd think my supervisor would notice that I'm basically running the whole department single-handedly during those long months, but he just ignores it. But yeah, to answer your question, almost the whole ten months has been that elevated, energetic phase, with just a few short breaks sprinkled in.

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a 10-month history of persistent delusions (coworkers/vendors tampering with data) and auditory hallucinations (a running commentary voice) that have remained continuously present regardless of mood state, including during clearly documented euthymic periods lasting several weeks (normal sleep, no irritability, no grandiosity) where psychotic symptoms persisted unabated. Superimposed on this psychotic process are distinct manic episodes meeting full criteria: decreased need for sleep, increased energy, grandiosity (belief he can 'overhaul the entire retail system' and see connections others cannot), irritability with angry outbursts, and increased goal-directed activity, occupying the majority of the 10-month period. Because psychotic symptoms occur both during mood episodes and during intervening periods of normal mood, and mood episodes are present for a substantial portion of the total illness duration, this pattern is diagnostic of Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type (F25.0) rather than Bipolar Disorder with psychotic features (which would require psychosis only during mood episodes) or Schizophrenia (which would not account for the prominent, criteria-meeting manic episodes).
